title: Shopping at the market — and saying no
goal: Ask prices, ask for quantities, and pay — and install a rule with no match in any language you probably know: the moment a sentence is NEGATIVE, the noun changes form.
bekal: ask prices with *Koliko stane?* and *Koliko stanejo?*
ask for quantities: *en kilogram*, *pol kile*, *deset dek*
switch the object to the Genitive as soon as the sentence is negative: *Imam kavo* → *Nimam kave*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Na Centralni tržnici
dialogs.intro: Saturday morning at Ljubljana's central market. Budi stands in front of a fruit stall; the vendor knows the face of a foreigner who's just started learning.

lines.speaker: Prodajalka:
lines.id: Here you go! What can I get you?

lines.speaker: Prodajalka:
lines.id: Two euros a kilo. They're all local.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Potem prosim en kilogram. In tri banane.
lines.id: Then a kilo, please. And three bananas.
lines.literal: then please one kilogram. and three bananas.

lines.speaker: Prodajalka:
lines.id: Anything else? We have lovely tomatoes.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Pol kile, prosim. Koliko je vse skupaj?
lines.id: Half a kilo, please. How much is that altogether?
lines.literal: half of-kilo, please. how-much is all together?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Oprostite, nimam drobiža. Lahko plačam s kartico?
lines.id: Sorry, I don't have any change. Can I pay by card?
lines.literal: sorry, I-not-have of-change. can I-pay with card?

lines.speaker: Prodajalka:
lines.id: Not at the market, cash only.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: V redu, bankomat je blizu. Takoj se vrnem.
lines.id: OK, the ATM is close. I'll be right back.
lines.literal: in order, ATM is near. right-away self I-return.

lines.speaker: Prodajalka:
lines.id: No problem, I'll wait for you.

notes: **Kaj bo dobrega?** literally "what will be of the good?" — a typical market vendor's greeting, roughly "What can I get you?". You don't need to copy it, but you do need to recognize it, because it'll be the first thing you hear at every stall.
**Stane or stanejo — it follows the number of items.** *Koliko stane kruh?* (one thing) but *Koliko stanejo jabolka?* (several things). That's exactly like English *how much is / how much are*.

**Prices are given in the object form.** *Stane štiri evre* — not *štiri evri*. The reason: the item "costs" an amount, and that amount is treated as an object. From five up the form goes back to the Genitive: *pet evrov*, *deset evrov*, *petdeset centov*.

**Nimam drobiža — this is the heart of the unit.** In an ordinary sentence you say *Imam drobiž* (I have change). As soon as the sentence is negative, the noun switches to the Genitive: *Nimam drobiž**a***. Slovenian thinks it makes sense that something absent is named with an "of" form — and after a few weeks, you'll agree.

**Samo gotovina.** At Slovenia's open-air markets cards often aren't accepted — and in most small towns, shops are completely closed on Sundays. Knowing both facts from the start saves many a Saturday morning: get cash first, shop on Saturday, leave nothing for Sunday.

grammars.title: The Genitive of negation — the big rule of this unit
body: In Slovenian, saying no isn't just adding *ne*. The noun changes form too — from the **tožilnik** (Accusative, the object) to the **rodilnik** (Genitive). The rule has no exceptions, and it applies in every negative sentence that has an object.
after: The Genitive form is exactly the same as the form after *iz* in unit 2: feminine words end in **-e** (*kava* → *kave*), masculine and neuter words end in **-a** (*čas* → *časa*, *pivo* → *piva*).

Look at the fourth row: for **living** masculine words, the Accusative and Genitive forms are twins from the start (*brata* for both), so the negative sentence doesn't change at all. One group of words that asks nothing of you.

grammars.title: Prices and money
body: Slovenia's currency has been the euro since 2007. All you need to learn is how numbers attach to it — and that's the same pattern as in unit 5.
after: The last row shows an everyday habit: cents are often **not mentioned at all**. *Tri evre in dvajset* is understood as €3.20. In writing, Slovenia uses a comma for cents: **3,20 €**, not a point as in English.

Sentences to learn whole: *Koliko stane?* (how much is it), *Koliko je vse skupaj?* (how much altogether), *Je to popust?* (is this on sale?), *Lahko plačam s kartico?* (can I pay by card), *Prosim račun* (the receipt, please).

grammars.title: Quantities at the market
body: One Slovenian habit that surprises newcomers: small quantities are counted in **deka** — units of ten grams, an Austrian legacy that lives on all over Central Europe.
after: When you order cheese or cold cuts, don't say grams — say **deka**. *Dvajset dek sira, prosim* = "two hundred grams of cheese". Saying "dvesto gramov" will be understood, but it instantly marks you as a foreigner.
Notice *pol kile*: after *pol* (half), the noun takes the Genitive — just like after numbers from five up. Every quantity word in Slovenian behaves this way.

sections.title: Sadje in zelenjava — fruit and vegetables

blocks.text: Fruit and vegetable names are the vocabulary you'll put to use fastest, because you'll say them every week. The third column shows the form you use when ordering more than one.
Notice **jabolko** is said **YAH-bohw-koh** — the *l* in the middle turns into *u*, as usual. And the form for five and up, *jabolk*, loses its ending entirely; that's normal for neuter words.
**Grozdje** (grapes) and **korenje** (carrots) are collective nouns: they have no plural, like English "rice". You always buy *pol kile grozdja*, never "five grapes".

blocks.title: Words that help you at the stall
items: *domač* (doh-MAHCH) — local produce, not imported. The most powerful sales word at a Slovenian market.
*Lahko poskusim?* — Can I try some? At a Slovenian market, the answer is almost always yes.

blocks.text: A handful of sentences that cover almost every small transaction — at the market, at the corner shop, or at a kiosk.

*Samo gledam* (just looking) is a lifesaver in clothing stores: Slovenian shop assistants usually greet you as soon as you walk in, and this sentence closes the conversation kindly without you having to say more.

One thing to plan for: **on Sundays, Slovenia is closed**. Since 2024 most large stores must close on Sundays, and in small towns almost everything does. The only things open are gas stations, small kiosks at stations, and a few shops in tourist centers. Do your shopping on Saturday.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with the right form of evro.
Wave review — unit 5. Translate into Slovenian without looking back at the unit.

answers: Nimam denarja. — Nimam časa. — Ne pijem kave. — Tukaj ni piva. — Nimam drobiža. — Ne kupim solate.
evro — evra — evre — evrov — evrov — centov
Koliko stanejo jabolka? — En kilogram, prosim. — Pol kile paradižnikov. — Koliko je vse skupaj? — Lahko plačam s kartico? — Nimam drobiža.
Star sem triindvajset let. — Imam dve sestri. — Koliko knjig? — Pet knjig. — Koliko ljudi je tukaj?
